explanation: No clear shared feature. Top examples are a mix: digits inside years and model numbers (the '0' in 2008, '2' in 20.04, RTX 2060), finance and market wording (rate, stock closed, interest, financial, 'below the' forecast), and pieces of proper names (Hokkaido, WeChat, Badminton, Liang). Mid and weak examples look random.

Fires on subword pieces in the middle of technical or rare words, mostly biomedical and chemical terms (thym-id-ilat, de-hydr-atase, nucle-ot-ides, Sac-char-omyces) and odd proper names (Cheyney, Chikushino, MississIPpi). It also fires on Ruby block ' do' and on some code tokens. Plain common words get only weak activation.

Fires on a token that completes or extends a noun phrase near the start of a news lead or abstract: the head noun or word after an adjective ('Florida teenager', 'eight-year-old boy', 'agent who', 'home page', 'economic and'). It is a diffuse position-in-phrase signal and does not depend on any particular token.

Fires in source code on a variable or identifier being used, mostly right after '=', 'return' or '(' in an expression, for example 'string = string.replace', 'this.Name = name', 'return res'. The strongest cases reuse a variable that was just defined. It fires weakly on code tokens outside such expressions and does not fire on prose.

Fires on a verb, participle or preposition that links a noun to a following agent or object phrase. By far the strongest single case is 'governing' in the Apache license line 'specific language governing permissions'. Others: 'noise coming from', 'exception occurred', 'played by', 'secreted', 'produced by'.

Fires on time-period words that finish a relative time expression, above all 'year' in 'last year' or 'this year' ('this year's', 'last year's'), and also 'season' and 'fiscal year'. It also fires on the last digit of a year or decade (194[2], 198[0]s). Other dates such as weekday names fire only moderately.

Mixed. It fires strongly on 'view' in 'please view the LICENSE' and 'in full view', on 'ostensibly' or 'seemingly', on 'rigid' or 'rig', on 'complex', and on 'from' after verbs of preventing ('stop X from'). These look like several unrelated lexical triggers.

Fires on a subword fragment in the middle of a word that is split into several tokens, for example search[eng]ineland, here[ina]fter, post-trans[l]ational, supern[at]ant, Concent[r]ations, Holy[ro]od. The token is never a whole word, and it fires most when the split is unusual. It does not fire on whole words.

Fires on calls to action aimed at the reader in blog, web-page or UI text: 'if you [like/enjoyed] this post', 'Click the button to', share, print and download buttons, 'Story continues below', 'External links'. The top two examples ('if you like', 'if you enjoyed') are much stronger than the rest.

Fires on the first subword of a word that the tokenizer splits, mostly biomedical terms (creat-inine, am-niotomy, am-ebocyte, ser-ine, Respir-atory) plus a few others (read-ym-ade, hone-ym-oons, M-DF, r-ingleader). It fires on the word-start piece of a multi-token word, with a bias toward medical and chemical vocabulary.

Fires on the second word of a technical compound or set phrase, where the token is the head term after a modifier: 'greatest common', 'lowest common', 'default constructor', 'Coma Scale', 'wrongful discharge', 'ground floor', 'layout_margin', 'pulsed-field gel'. The phrases come from many domains, especially code and math.

Fires on the second or later subword of a proper name that the tokenizer splits, mainly person names (Rich-mond, Ab-dess-amad, Tom-my, Rodrig-uez, Abd-ullah, Huckabee) and also brand names and acronyms (NO-AA, Trip-Advisor, L-GPL, LL-VM, MS-DN). Ordinary words fire weakly.

Mixed. It fires on programming terms (Xcode, 'template <class/typename>', typescript, monads, directive), on biochemical word endings (prostaglandin, phenylalanine, synovial, reticulum), and on legal-citation boilerplate ('ATTORNEY FOR', 'representatives of', 'P.A.'). There is no single shared feature.

Fires on a word in the middle of a running prose sentence, often in comparisons or quantities ('more importance', 'far less attention', 'More women', 'less money', 'most people') and on prepositions and articles after them. It is a diffuse feature with no clearly predictable trigger.

Fires on the surname or second name part of a person's or place's name, right after the first name or first token: 'Michael E. Broadway', 'Jimmy Hastings', 'William Aberhart', 'Marcus Cannon', 'Trou-sdale Estates'. It is strongest in legal case captions and the openings of encyclopedia entries. Common words fire weakly.

Fires on words in physics and math writing, especially condensed-matter terms ('metal', 'metallic', 'ground state', 'lattice', 'liquid crystal') and LaTeX syntax tokens ('}{', '\text', '\frac{', '\limits'). It fires on technical tokens in scientific or mathematical text.

Fires on verbs of speaking or interviewing in interview-style text ('got to speak/talk with', 'I spoke to', 'had the good fortune of speaking with', 'questionnaires', 'Thematic analysis of interviews'). It also fires on the first letter of an email or handle after '@' or 'at' and on some Danish and Portuguese words.

No coherent pattern. The top examples include 'subject to', 'map.addLayer', commas before quotes or clauses, 'StackExchange', 'chronically', 'said that', 'tied for', 'less likely'. These are mixed tokens from many contexts.

Fires on words for a relationship or connection between two parties, usually after 'the two' or 'both': 'parted ways', 'tied the knot', 'double date', 'remained friends', 'closely related', 'sever ties', 'both sides', 'joined', 'interact', 'interlink'. The strongest cases describe two people or two entities being linked or separated.

Fires on the first token of a new paragraph that begins body text, usually right after a title or heading line and a blank line ('[I] am', '[It] took', '[The] overarching', Russian '[В]'). The token itself barely matters: a sentence-initial word right after '\n\n' at the start of the body fires strongly, while the same word inside a paragraph does not.

No clear pattern. It fires on tokens in non-English text (Hungarian, Albanian, Portuguese), music-related words (melody, timbres, Subtone), and assorted English mid-sentence words ('sports', 'and', 'that', 'of', 'game').
